overview: This single-page Department of State “List of Papers” inventories documents numbered 71–78 filed under decimal 894.77 concerning Japanese railways, railway construction, equipment, industrial intelligence, and wartime transportation controls. The entries describe or cross-reference intercepted Japanese diplomatic despatches from Colombia, confidential Justice Department information, Japanese and Manchukuo yearbooks and government railway reports obtained through a Westinghouse representative, construction of a high-speed trunk line between Tokyo and Shimonoseki, railway loadings, foreign-broadcast intelligence, and restrictions on passenger traffic in Japan, chiefly during 1942 and the surrounding wartime period.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers for decimal file 894.77
subfiles.about: An administrative index summarizes papers and cross-references concerning Japanese railway construction, operations, equipment, and wartime traffic restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The list records papers numbered 71–78, including intercepted diplomatic despatches, confidential intelligence, railway yearbooks and annual reports, telegrams, and broadcast-monitoring material. Its principal railway subjects are a proposed high-speed trunk line between Tokyo and Shimonoseki, railway loadings in Japan, and restrictions on passenger traffic. Several entries direct researchers to other decimal files, while the 1942 entries identify military-intelligence and Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service sources.

interest: The page is useful as a roadmap to a dispersed body of wartime intelligence on Japan’s transport system, showing how the State Department combined diplomatic interception, corporate contacts, official Japanese publications, confidential informants, and broadcast monitoring. Particularly notable are the references to the unrealized Tokyo–Shimonoseki high-speed trunk railway and to railway loadings and passenger restrictions, subjects that can illuminate wartime infrastructure planning and transport capacity. The entry naming Fred Thomas also documents the use of an American industrial representative as a source for Japanese and Manchukuo railway publications.
